clue.text: Alice rewritten for Gilbertian fairy

indicators.note: a name rewritten has its letters set down again in a new order

explanation.surface: A heroine's name is reworked to suit a Gilbert and Sullivan character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewritten' rearranges the letters of ALICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Celia is one of the fairies in Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta Iolanthe.

clue.text: She continued a saga from absolute zero

definitions.text: She continued a saga from absolute zero

parts.words: She continued a saga from absolute zero
parts.note: absolute zero sounds like physics but is a book title in a children's family saga by a woman novelist

explanation.surface: A woman resumed a long story starting from nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Helen Cresswell's Bagthorpe Saga continues with the book Absolute Zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Helen Cresswell wrote the Bagthorpe Saga, whose second book is Absolute Zero.

clue.text: Greek mites destroy plate

indicators.note: to destroy the word is to break up its letters and remake them

explanation.surface: Tiny creatures ruin a piece of crockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroy' rearranges PLATE. 'mites' are small coins, not insects.
explanation.definitionFit: Lepta were small Greek coins, the widow's mites of the Gospel story.

clue.text: God in a changed Libyan city of Byzantine ruins

parts.note: Apollo is a Greek god

indicators.note: the two short words are changed in order of letters

explanation.surface: A deity appears in a transformed North African city of ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' acts only on the two words after the god's name; Apollonia was the port of ancient Cyrene.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollonia was the port of Cyrene in Libya, known for its Byzantine remains.

clue.text: Fast character identified by copper Greek city's sheltering

indicators.note: the city's name holds the metal symbol inside it, as a shelter covers what it protects

parts.note: Sparta is the ancient Greek city; with its 's it gives SPARTAS
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A policeman is spotted in a Greek city where he had taken refuge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speed but is the novelist Howard Fast; 'copper' looks like a policeman but is the element. 'sheltering' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Howard Fast wrote the novel Spartacus about the gladiator who led a slave revolt against Rome.

clue.text: Artist's vest

definitions.meaning: Stanley ... was an English painter; the 's stands for 'is'
a short close-fitting jacket or undervest

explanation.surface: A painter's undergarment.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Spencer was the painter of Cookham, and a spencer is also a short garment worn on the upper body.

clue.text: Mortimer suggested conflicting ones

parts.note: a character called Mortimer proposed replies that contradicted each other

explanation.surface: Someone named Mortimer offered contradictory replies.
explanation.definitionFit: Replies to questions are what conflicting ones would be.

clue.text: Short time to listen to farce

parts.note: T is short for time
hark means to listen

explanation.surface: A brief pause to hear a comic play.
explanation.walkthrough: Thark is a 1927 Aldwych farce by Ben Travers.
explanation.definitionFit: Thark is one of Ben Travers's Aldwych farces, staged in London in the 1920s.

clue.text: One who foresaw first careless fool and academician

indicators.note: the first letter of the word careless is taken

parts.note: an ass is a fool
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: A careless idiot and a scholar saw what was coming.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassandra was the Trojan prophetess whose predictions were never believed.

clue.text: Rumoured to betray Irish dramatist

indicators.note: rumoured means as heard said, so the word is matched by its sound

parts.note: to sing is slang for informing on someone, to betray them

explanation.surface: Gossip says someone will inform on an Irish playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rumoured' matches the slang SING with the playwright's name.
explanation.definitionFit: J. M. Synge wrote The Playboy of the Western World for Dublin's Abbey Theatre.

clue.text: Mazo de la Roche's were up betimes for a look round

definitions.text: Mazo de la Roche's were up betimes for a look round

parts.words: Mazo de la Roche's were up betimes for a look round
parts.note: betimes means early, at dawn: the clue points to the Canadian novelist's book whose title has people out at dawn looking about them

explanation.surface: A novelist's characters rose early to look about them.
explanation.walkthrough: Mazo de la Roche wrote Explorers of the Dawn; 'up betimes' is the dawn, and explorers are people out for a look round.
explanation.definitionFit: People who travel to look over new ground are explorers, and de la Roche's book title names them at dawn.

clue.text: Russell child is Argonaut's father

parts.note: the Irish poet George Russell wrote under the pen name AE
a son is a child

explanation.surface: A child of a man named Russell turns out to be the father of a Greek hero.
explanation.walkthrough: George Russell signed his poems AE, a fact a literary solver may know.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Aeson was the father of Jason, leader of the Argonauts.

clue.text: Least sort of hostess, inconstant, but reportedly with constant lover

definitions.text: hostess, inconstant, but reportedly with constant lover

indicators.note: to sort the word is to put its letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A fickle salon hostess is said to have had a faithful lover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges LEAST. 'constant' plays on Benjamin Constant, the writer who was her lover.
explanation.definitionFit: Madame de Staël kept a famous Paris salon and had a long affair with Benjamin Constant.

clue.text: Control partner in ballet

parts.note: to check something is to control or restrain it
a mate is a partner

explanation.surface: A dancer keeps a firm hold of a partner during a ballet.
explanation.definitionFit: Checkmate is a one-act ballet with music by Arthur Bliss, choreographed by Ninette de Valois.

clue.text: Lioness in winter?

parts.note: plays on the play and film The Lion in Winter: the lion is Henry II, and the lioness is his queen

explanation.surface: A big cat endures the cold season.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lion in Winter is James Goldman's play about Henry II; his wife is the royal lioness.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry II's queen in the play was Eleanor of Aquitaine, as fierce as her husband.

clue.text: See unclad, dishevelled, conspiratorial giant

indicators.note: dishevelled means messed up, so the letters are put in disorder

explanation.surface: A scruffy, naked giant plotting is spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dishevelled' rearranges SEE UNCLAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Enceladus was one of the Giants who plotted war against the Olympian gods.

clue.text: Second loan-shark seen in Windsor Park

parts.note: a loan-shark is a money lender

explanation.surface: A second moneylender has been spotted in the park at Windsor.
explanation.walkthrough: Slender is a foolish suitor in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor, whose last act is set in Windsor Park.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham Slender is a character in The Merry Wives of Windsor, present at the final scene in Windsor Park.

clue.text: "A traveller has a right to relate and his adventures as he pleases" (Raspe)

definitions.text: "A traveller has a right to relate and his adventures as he pleases" (Raspe)

parts.words: "A traveller has a right to relate and his adventures as he pleases" (Raspe)
parts.note: a quotation from Raspe's Baron Munchausen with one verb missing, meaning to adorn a tale with made-up detail

explanation.surface: A line from the Munchausen tales with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Baron Munchausen claims a traveller may dress up his adventures however he likes.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress up a story with invented decoration is to adorn it.

clue.text: Would-be bigamist from Kentish Town

definitions.meaning: Mr ... in Jane Eyre tries to marry Jane while his first wife lives
A cathedral city in the English county of Kent

explanation.surface: A man who nearly married twice comes from a district of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Kentish Town is also a district of London, which misleads; here it means a town in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Rochester of Jane Eyre nearly commits bigamy, and Rochester is a town in Kent.

clue.text: Benson protagonist not applicable as Adriana's sister

parts.note: E. F. Benson's comic novels centre on Lucia

explanation.surface: A novel's heroine is said to be irrelevant as a sister.
explanation.walkthrough: Lucia is the snobbish heroine of E. F. Benson's Mapp and Lucia novels.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors Luciana is the sister of Adriana.

clue.text: Lorry the French used for piece in journal

parts.note: an artic is an articulated lorry, a British term for a large truck
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A French truck is used for a newspaper story.
explanation.walkthrough: A lorry is the British word for a truck; ARTIC is short for articulated lorry.
explanation.definitionFit: An article is a written item in a newspaper or magazine.

clue.text: "Bent, but not broken, with age" was Evangeline's' notary

definitions.text: "Bent, but not broken, with age" was Evangeline's' notary

parts.words: "Bent, but not broken, with age" was Evangeline's' notary
parts.note: quotes Longfellow's description of the old village lawyer in his poem Evangeline

explanation.surface: An aged lawyer is described as bowed but unbroken.
explanation.walkthrough: In Longfellow's Evangeline the notary René Leblanc is 'bent, but not broken, by age'.
explanation.definitionFit: René Leblanc is the notary public of Grand-Pré in Longfellow's poem.

clue.text: Circular tract

definitions.meaning: a circular is a printed notice sent round to many people
a tract is a short pamphlet

explanation.surface: A round stretch of land.
explanation.definitionFit: A printed handout is both a circular and a tract, a short pamphlet.

clue.text: A pale star suffering in the gym

indicators.note: a star in distress is pictured as knocked about, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A washed-out celebrity is having a hard time at the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffering' rearranges A PALE STAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A palaestra was an ancient Greek wrestling school, a training ground for athletes.

clue.text: Titanic output observed from this poet

definitions.text: Titanic output observed from this poet

parts.words: Titanic output observed from this poet
parts.note: titanic looks like huge but names a narrative poem about the lost liner by a Canadian poet

explanation.surface: A poet produced an enormous body of work.
explanation.walkthrough: E. J. Pratt, a Canadian poet, wrote the long poem The Titanic.
explanation.definitionFit: E. J. Pratt's narrative poem The Titanic recounts the 1912 sinking.

clue.text: Additional charge for minor character

definitions.meaning: a walk-on actor with no lines

explanation.surface: A small part in a film costs more.
explanation.definitionFit: A surcharge on a bill and a walk-on film actor are both called extras.

clue.text: "Stubb was lustily singing out for someone to him up" (Moby Dick)

definitions.text: "Stubb was lustily singing out for someone to him up" (Moby Dick)

parts.words: "Stubb was lustily singing out for someone to him up" (Moby Dick)
parts.note: a quotation from Melville with one word missing: the verb for serving a portion with a big spoon

explanation.surface: A line from Melville with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Stubb, the second mate, is calling for someone to serve him up a helping.
explanation.definitionFit: To serve someone up a helping with a big spoon is to dish it out to them.

clue.text: Associated with Miller by James, and with Burns by Kavanagh

definitions.text: Associated with Miller by James, and with Burns by Kavanagh

parts.words: Associated with Miller by James, and with Burns by Kavanagh
parts.note: two novel titles that pair one first name with two surnames, by Henry James and Julia Kavanagh

explanation.surface: Names linked with a miller and with burns.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry James wrote Daisy Miller and Julia Kavanagh wrote Daisy Burns.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James's Daisy Miller and Julia Kavanagh's Daisy Burns share the heroine's first name.

clue.text: Evaluation from Rupert of Hentzau, ditching the evidence

indicators.note: the answer is taken out from inside the run of words that follows the title

explanation.surface: An assessment of a Ruritanian villain leaves out the evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across 'HentzAU DITching'. Rupert of Hentzau is Anthony Hope's sequel to The Prisoner of Zenda.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is a formal check of accounts, an official evaluation.

clue.text: California puts French wine first for reformer

parts.note: vin is French for wine
1st, written IST, is the abbreviation for first

explanation.surface: A Californian sets French wine ahead of everything for a religious reformer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' looks like an order to put the wine first but gives 1ST, read as IST.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of John Calvin's Protestant doctrines belongs to the Reformation tradition.

clue.text: Muddled statement by Hutchinson

indicators.note: a muddled statement has its letters jumbled into a different order

explanation.surface: A confused remark is attributed to someone called Hutchinson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muddled' rearranges STATEMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Testament is a 1938 novel by R. C. Hutchinson.

clue.text: Her material was light and romantic, like georgette

definitions.text: Her material was light and romantic, like georgette

parts.words: Her material was light and romantic, like georgette
parts.note: georgette is a light silk fabric, but here it is the first name of a novelist who wrote light Regency romances

explanation.surface: A dressmaker's fabric was flimsy and pretty.
explanation.walkthrough: Georgette Heyer wrote popular Regency romance novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Georgette Heyer's novels are light historical romances.
